The interpreters' comments on the word άγχιστον [nearest] are vain, rightly criticized by Meineke in Philologus vol. 20 p. 71, who conjectured ἀρχηγὸν [leader], comparing the words of the chorus leader that immediately follow, ἥκω σεβίζων σόν, Κλυταιμνήστρα, κράτος· δίκη γάρ ἐστι φωτὸς ἀρχηγοῦ τίειν | γυναῖκ᾽ ἐρημωθέντος ἄρσενος θρόνου [I come honoring your power, Clytemnestra; for it is right to honor the wife of a leader when the male throne is empty], which are as a paraphrase of the previous words. And rightly, I think, Meineke judged the sense of the word written by Aeschylus. But since it is hardly probable that the well-known word ἀρχηγόν [leader] was corrupted into ἄγχιστον [nearest], it seems better to write ἄρχιστον [supreme], which no one will wonder was changed into ἄγχιστον [nearest]. With this restored, a most apt meaning emerges, by which the supreme power is said to be now in Clytemnestra's hands. ἄρχιστος [supreme] is formed from ἀρχός [leader] as βασιλεύτατος [most kingly] from βασιλεύς [king] and others of this kind, about which see the Thesaurus vol. 2 p. 168. More remarkable is ἀρχέστατος [most ancient] (for αρχαιότατος [most ancient], as it seems, accepted by grammarians), which Philoxenus cites from Aeschylus' Penelope in Etym. M. p. 31, 5.
